anecdote

AN-ik-doht -- three syllables, stress on the first syllable, AN. Careful: it is anecdote, not 'antidote' -- the cure for a poison. · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Anecdote is a short, entertaining story about a real incident.

Every long car trip ends with Uncle Ray's anecdote about the runaway shopping cart.

Example

Amara's college-essay draft is all numbers: 'I tutored for 120 hours and helped 14 students.' Her older brother, home from college, reads it over her shoulder. 'Tell me about one of them.' So she adds a three-sentence anecdote about the evening Jonah, who hated math, taught her a shortcut he had invented -- and suddenly the essay breathes.

An anecdote is a short account of one real moment. Writers and speakers prize anecdotes because a single true story lands harder than a page of statistics -- but remember that anecdotes are only single cases; 'anecdotal evidence' is the phrase for stories doing a job that really needs data.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

tale: A tale leans toward the invented: fairy tales, folk tales, tall tales -- 'telling tales' even means lying. An anecdote points the opposite way: it is a short account of something that really happened, offered as true.

recollection: A recollection is a memory put into words -- something you call back from your own past and report. An anecdote is more performed: a short, entertaining account of a real incident, shaped to amuse listeners, whether or not it happened to the teller.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

epic: a long, sweeping story

saga: a long, detailed chain of events

Where it sits · how carefully crafted the telling is

story → anecdote → vignette

story vs. anecdote: Story asks the least of the three: any account of events, true or invented, long or short, counts as a story, while an anecdote is at least chosen and trimmed -- one real incident kept short enough to entertain.

vignette vs. anecdote: Vignette is the strongest and most crafted: an anecdote is casually told for interest or laughs, but a vignette has been polished like a miniature painting, every detail placed on purpose.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — an-: not (Greek)

prefix — ec-: out (Greek ek-, spelled ec- in English)

root — dote: given (from Greek dotos, from didonai, 'to give')

Put it together: Anecdote is Greek for 'things not given out' -- an- ('not') + ec- ('out') + dote ('given', from Greek dotos): the unpublished stories. The historian Procopius titled his secret, gossipy history of the emperor's court 'Anekdota' -- the tales too juicy to publish. An anecdote is still exactly that: the small true story that never makes the official record, told across a dinner table instead.

Use the root in a new word: antidote: The ranger's kit carries an antidote for the canyon's one venomous snake.

Strength Check

Word Choice

An anecdote is short, entertaining, and true (or at least told as true) -- a real moment, not an invented plot. Speakers open with anecdotes, essays turn on them, and grandparents polish the same ones for decades. Two cautions: don't confuse it with antidote (the remedy for a poison -- the words differ by two letters), and treat 'anecdotal evidence' as a warning label: one good story is not the same as proof.
